source.title: Interpretable and Steerable Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Akshay R. Kulkarni; T. Weng; V. Narayanaswamy; Shu-Sen Liu; W. Sakla; Kowshik Thopalli

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports measurements on sparse-autoencoder latent features in vision models, not on the original network's neuron poles or on the claim versions' stated tests. It does not test or rely on those claims.
record.gate_note: The paper measures interpretability and steerability of SAE features using CLIP-Dissect and downstream steering. These are related to, but not measurements of, whether a model's own neuron poles have one or two main jobs. It does not test explanations on held-out activating examples or score predictions on new text. Referenced results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study scores sparse-autoencoder latents trained on vision encoders (CLIP-ViT-L, DINOv2-L) for CLIP-Dissect interpretability and downstream steerability. It does not measure how many of a model's own neurons have one or two main jobs. It does not examine InceptionV1, attribute neuron messiness to architecture, build neuron-based circuits, or score explanations by simulating activations. It cites Bills et al. only as an example of autointerpretability scoring. The one native-neuron number, the mean steerability of CLIP layer-22 neurons (0.173), is a steering score with no interpretability share, so it fits no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find most SAE latents low in interpretability, steerability or both, and SAE concept coverage incomplete. They propose CB-SAE, which prunes low-utility latents and adds a concept bottleneck, and report average gains of +32.1% in interpretability and +14.5% in steerability.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures vision SAE feature scores using CLIP-Dissect and steering outputs; it does not use the neuron-explanation evaluation method or neuron-pole analysis in the claim's source studies.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported category shares change when the steerability threshold changes from the SAE mean to the original model's average score (0.173). The paper also varies the CLIP-like model used for interpretability evaluation and reports different raw scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Only 12–20% of SAE latents on vision encoders score above the mean on both CLIP-Dissect interpretability and downstream steerability. With the native-neuron steerability baseline (0.173) as the threshold, the share is 29%. A 65,536-latent SAE misses 27–45% of ImageNet-derived concepts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Most vision-encoder SAE latents are not both interpretable and steerable, and SAE concept coverage is incomplete, with shares depending on thresholds and the downstream model.

fits_no_version.finding: The native CLIP layer-22 neurons have a mean steerability of 0.173, below the SAE latents' mean of 0.232 (Appendix C.3). No interpretability share is given for the native neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Native vision-encoder neurons steer LLaVA outputs less well than SAE latents do, on average.

record.problems: The study evaluates SAE latent features rather than native network neuron poles. Its interpretability measure relies on CLIP-Dissect and its steerability score is an indirect downstream similarity metric. The category split depends on score thresholds; the paper reports materially different proportions under an alternate steerability threshold. No uncertainty estimates for these proportions are stated.

untested.parts: All of it: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole shares (one job, two jobs, not understood).
All of it: shares in other language models, dense and mixture-of-experts, at scale.
All of it: InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization versus superposition.
All of it: whether architecture, regularization or tools drive the share of interpretable native neurons.
All of it: neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model.
All of it: whether explanations that fit activating examples fail to predict firing.
All of it: simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations on new text.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'discusses' overstates the link. The paper never addresses the claim or its essay; it cites Bills et al. only as an autointerpretability method. Its 'neurons' are SAE latents throughout. CB-SAE gains (Tables 1–6) are the paper's own method results and rightly are not rows.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole proportions and one- versus two-job judgments.
Cross-model and scale claims for language models, dense or mixture-of-experts models, and models up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Whether architecture, regularization, or tools cause changes in the share of interpretable native network neurons; the stated InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and whether they explain behavior without a replacement model.
Whether explanations fit activating examples but fail to predict where neurons fire.
Automated simulation scores for neuron explanations on new text.
